The court

What Is First Parish Court in Jefferson Parish?

A limited-jurisdiction trial court serving the East Bank: civil suits up to $50,000, misdemeanours, first and second offence DWI, and traffic.

First Parish Court is a limited-jurisdiction trial court that serves the East Bank of Jefferson Parish, Louisiana. It hears civil lawsuits where the amount in dispute is $50,000 or less, misdemeanour criminal cases, first and second-offence DWI, and traffic matters. The court sits at 924 David Drive in Metairie and operates two divisions, Division A and Division B, each presided over by an elected judge.

For most residents of Metairie, Kenner, Harahan, River Ridge, and Jefferson, First Parish Court is the courthouse they are most likely to walk into: a traffic ticket, a security deposit dispute, an eviction, a small contract disagreement. It is the court closest to everyday life.

Jurisdiction

What cases does First Parish Court hear?

Four dockets, all of them the ordinary business of the East Bank.

Docket 01 · Civil

Civil cases up to $50,000

The court's civil docket covers disputes where the damages sought are $50,000 or less. In practice, that means:

  • Security deposit and landlord-tenant disputes
  • Evictions and rule for possession
  • Unpaid invoices, contracts, and small business collections
  • Property damage from minor auto accidents
  • Consumer disputes with contractors and repair shops

Because the dollar limit is comparatively low, most people in these cases are representing themselves or working with counsel for the first time. How clearly a judge explains the process matters enormously here.

Docket 02 · Criminal

Misdemeanour criminal cases

First Parish Court handles misdemeanours arising on the East Bank, including theft under $750, shoplifting under $500, disturbing the peace and simple battery.

Docket 03 · DWI

DWI, first and second offence

First and second offence DWI charges are heard in First Parish Court. Third and subsequent offences are felonies and go to the 24th Judicial District Court.

Docket 04 · Traffic

Traffic

Traffic citations issued on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish are handled here, including violations connected to traffic accidents. The court operates a traffic hearing process to resolve routine citations without a full trial.

Where your case goes

First Parish Court and the other Jefferson Parish courts

CourtWhat it handles
First Parish CourtEast Bank: civil cases up to $50,000, misdemeanours, DWI first and second offences, traffic.
Second Parish CourtThe same categories on the West Bank of Jefferson Parish.
24th Judicial District CourtFelonies, civil suits above the parish court limit, family and succession matters.
Justice of the Peace CourtsVery small civil claims and certain local matters within a ward.

If you received a citation or a lawsuit and are not sure which courthouse to go to, the address printed on your paperwork is authoritative.

Divisions

Divisions A and B

First Parish Court has two divisions. Each is led by a judge elected by voters on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish to a term of six years confirm.

Home/Court/Traffic tickets

Court explainer

Jefferson Parish Traffic Tickets: What Happens Next

Your case generally goes to First Parish Court at 924 David Drive. You generally have three options, and ignoring the ticket is the one that reliably makes it worse.

If you received a traffic citation on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish, your case generally goes to First Parish Court at 924 David Drive in Metairie. You generally have three options, and ignoring the ticket is the one choice that reliably makes the problem worse.

01

Pay the citation

Resolves the matter. For most moving violations it is treated as a conviction and may be reported to your insurer and to the OMV.

02

Contest it at a hearing

Faster and less formal than a trial, but still a legal proceeding, and what you say is on the record.

03

Appear on your court date

If your citation requires an appearance, go. Bring the citation, your licence, insurance, registration and anything supporting your defence.

01

Read the citation itself

Everything you need is on the ticket. Find these four things before you do anything else:

  • The court named on the ticket. East Bank citations go to First Parish Court. West Bank citations go to Second Parish Court. A citation from Louisiana State Police may go elsewhere.
  • Your appearance date. This is a deadline, not a suggestion.
  • The violation charged. Some violations can be resolved administratively. Others, including anything charged alongside a DWI, cannot.
  • The citation number. You will need it for every call and every payment.
02

Understand your options

Pay the citation

Paying resolves the matter and, for most moving violations, is treated as a conviction that may be reported to your insurer and to the Office of Motor Vehicles. Contact the Traffic Department at (504) 731-4682 for current amounts and accepted payment methods. confirm

Contest the citation

You may appear and contest the ticket. In First Parish Court, routine citations are often handled through a traffic hearing process rather than a full trial. A traffic hearing officer reviews the citation, hears from the driver and the issuing officer, and makes a recommendation to the court. It is faster and less formal than a trial, but it is still a legal proceeding and what you say is on the record.

Appear on your court date

If your citation requires a court appearance, go. Bring the citation, your licence, proof of insurance and registration, and any documentation relevant to your defence: a repair receipt, an inspection sticker, photographs of the intersection.

03

Know what happens if you do nothing

Missing your date is the expensive path. Depending on the violation, an unresolved citation can lead to additional fees, an attachment being issued, and a hold on your driver's licence renewal at the Office of Motor Vehicles. A ticket you could have handled for a modest amount becomes a much larger problem months later, usually at the worst possible moment.

If you have already missed a date, call the Traffic Department. Courts deal with this constantly, and addressing it voluntarily is treated differently from being picked up on an attachment.

The role

What a traffic hearing officer actually does

Most people have never heard the term until they get a ticket. A traffic hearing officer is appointed by the court to hear routine traffic matters, review the citation and the officer's account, listen to the driver, and make a recommendation. The volume is enormous; First Parish Court's traffic docket runs to thousands of matters a year, and the job is to move that volume without turning any person into a number.

Michael Marsiglia has served as Traffic Hearing Officer in First Parish Court for eleven years, overseeing more than 25,000 docketed matters. That is the single largest body of hands-on experience anyone can bring to this particular bench in this election. Both elected Judges for First Parish Court have appointed Michael to serve in this capacity.

11Years hearing traffic matters here
25,000+Docketed traffic matters overseen
This is a campaign website. It explains how the process generally works. It is not legal advice, it does not create an attorney-client relationship, and it cannot tell you how your case will come out. For advice about your own matter, speak with a Louisiana attorney. For scheduling and payment questions, call the court.

Frequently asked questions

Which court handles my Jefferson Parish traffic ticket?

Citations issued on the East Bank go to First Parish Court, 924 David Drive, Metairie. West Bank citations go to Second Parish Court.

Can I just pay my ticket online?

Payment options are handled by the court's Traffic Department at (504) 731-4682. Confirm the amount and method directly with the court rather than a third-party site.

What happens if I miss my court date for a traffic ticket?

You may face additional fees, an attachment, and a hold on your driver's licence renewal. Contact the court as soon as you realise you missed the date.

Do I need a lawyer for a traffic ticket?

For a routine citation, many people appear without one. If the citation carries a possible jail sentence, is charged with a DWI, or could affect a commercial licence, talk to an attorney.

Is a DWI handled in First Parish Court?

First and second offence DWI are heard in First Parish Court. Third and subsequent offences are felonies handled by the 24th Judicial District Court.

What are First Parish Court's hours?

Monday through Thursday, 8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.; Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., excluding legal holidays.

Home/Court/Small claims

Court explainer

Small Claims and Civil Suits in Jefferson Parish

If the amount in dispute is $50,000 or less and it happened on the East Bank, your case belongs in First Parish Court.

If someone owes you money, damaged your property, or kept a deposit they should have returned, and the amount in dispute is $50,000 or less, your case belongs in a Jefferson Parish parish court. On the East Bank that is First Parish Court, at 924 David Drive in Metairie. Claims above $50,000 go to the 24th Judicial District Court.

These are the cases that rarely make the news and matter enormously to the people in them. A contractor who took a deposit and never came back. A landlord holding a security deposit. A repair shop that made the problem worse. For most of the people standing at those counsel tables, it is the only time they will ever be in court.

Scope

What kinds of cases belong here

  • Security deposit disputes. Louisiana law sets out a landlord's obligation to return a deposit or itemise deductions within a set period after the lease ends.
  • Evictions and rules for possession. Landlord-tenant possession matters on the East Bank.
  • Unpaid invoices and contracts. Small business collections, service agreements, breached contracts.
  • Property damage. Minor auto accidents, damage to a fence or vehicle, damage caused by a contractor.
  • Consumer disputes. Work not performed, work performed badly, goods not delivered.

Process

How filing works

Six steps, and the two that decide most self-represented cases are naming the defendant correctly and bringing your paper in order.

Bring documents, not narrative. The contract, the invoices, the proof of payment, the messages, in date order.
01

Confirm you are in the right court and the right amount

East Bank of Jefferson Parish, $50,000 or less. If your claim is worth more, you can either file in district court or waive the excess to stay in parish court, a real strategic decision worth thinking through, and one worth asking a lawyer about.

02

Identify the defendant correctly

This is where self-represented plaintiffs most often lose before they start. You need the correct legal name and a valid address for service. "The guy from the roofing company" is not a defendant. If the other side is a business, look up its registered agent through the Louisiana Secretary of State's business filings search.

03

File your petition with the Clerk

Contact the Civil Department at (504) 736-8391 for current forms and procedures. Filing fees change, so ask the Clerk what the current amount is rather than relying on a figure published anywhere. confirm

04

Serve the defendant

A lawsuit does not begin because you filed it. It begins when the other side is properly served. The Clerk's office handles service; make sure the address you provided is one where the defendant can actually be found.

05

Prepare your evidence

Bring documents, not narrative. The single best predictor of how a small civil case goes is whether the person brought paper:

  • The written contract, lease, work order or estimate
  • Invoices, receipts, and proof of payment, including cancelled cheques and card statements
  • Text messages and emails, printed out and in order by date
  • Photographs, dated where possible
  • A short written timeline for your own use
06

Show up

Cases are lost by non-appearance more than by anything a judge decides. If you cannot make a date, contact the court before the date, not after.

In the room

What to expect in the courtroom

Parish court is less formal than district court but it is still court. Arrive early, dress like you are going to a job interview, silence your phone, and address the judge as "Your Honour." Speak to the judge rather than to the other party. Answer the question you were asked. If you do not know something, say so.

Most importantly: bring your documents in an order you can find them in. A judge with a full docket cannot wait while you scroll through two years of text messages.

Why it matters

Why the judge matters in a $50,000 case

There is a temptation to think the stakes here are small. They are not. Fifty thousand dollars is years of rent, a working vehicle, or a small business's margin for the year. And in a court where many litigants have no lawyer, the judge's ability to run a fair, comprehensible, efficient proceeding is the quality of justice the person receives.

Michael Marsiglia has spent more than twenty years in civil litigation across Louisiana: contract disputes, construction litigation, insurance coverage, real estate, employment, probate and more, and has conducted over 300 court-appointed mediations. He has served First Parish Court as a Traffic Hearing Officer for eleven years and has been appointed by the Louisiana Supreme Court to sit there as Judge Pro Tempore.

Frequently asked questions

What is the maximum amount I can sue for in First Parish Court?

$50,000. Above that, the case goes to the 24th Judicial District Court.

Do I need a lawyer for a small claims case in Jefferson Parish?

No, you may represent yourself in a civil matter. Whether you should depends on the amount at stake and the complexity of the dispute.

Where do I file a small claims case on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish?

First Parish Court, 924 David Drive, Metairie, LA 70003. Civil Department: (504) 736-8391.

How long does a small civil case take in Jefferson Parish?

It varies with the docket, whether the defendant answers, and whether continuances are granted. Timelines are one of the main reasons docket management matters in a court like this one.

Are evictions handled in First Parish Court?

Yes. Landlord-tenant possession matters on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish are heard here.

Firm on the law. Fair to the people.

The seat on the ballot

First Parish Court, Division A

One of two divisions serving the East Bank. On the ballot in the open primary on Tuesday, November 3, 2026.

First Parish Court, Division A is one of two divisions of the court serving the East Bank of Jefferson Parish. The judge of Division A hears civil cases up to $50,000, misdemeanour criminal matters, first and second offence DWI, and traffic cases arising in Metairie, Kenner, Harahan, River Ridge, Jefferson and Elmwood. The seat is on the ballot in the open primary on Tuesday, November 3, 2026.

The work

What this judge actually decides

It is worth being concrete, because "parish court judge" sounds smaller than it is. In a given week, the judge of Division A may decide:

  • Whether a security deposit is returned
  • Whether a small business gets paid for work it performed
  • Whether a first-time DWI defendant goes to jail, to a programme, or home
  • Whether a traffic citation that could cost someone their commercial licence stands

Most of the people affected by these decisions will never appear before any other judge in their lives. Many of them will not have a lawyer. For them, this court is the justice system.

$50,000The civil ceiling
25,000+Matters Michael has heard here

The electorate

Who votes in this race

Voters registered on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish elect the judges of First Parish Court. If you live in Metairie, Kenner, Harahan, River Ridge, Jefferson, Elmwood or the surrounding East Bank communities, this seat is on your ballot. West Bank residents vote in Second Parish Court races instead.

Not sure whether this race is on your ballot? Check your personalised sample ballot through the Louisiana Secretary of State's GeauxVote portal, or contact the Jefferson Parish Registrar of Voters at (504) 736-6191.

How to vote on November 3

The candidacy

Michael Marsiglia's candidacy

  • Appointed by the Louisiana Supreme Court to sit as Judge Pro Tempore in First Parish Court
  • Eleven years as Traffic Hearing Officer in First Parish Court, overseeing more than 25,000 docketed matters
  • Ad Hoc Justice of the Peace for the Fifth Justice of the Peace Court in Jefferson Parish
  • More than 300 mediations as a court-appointed mediator for Louisiana district courts
  • Court-appointed curator in the 24th Judicial District Court
  • Over twenty years of civil and criminal practice, including service as counsel to the State of Louisiana, the Parish of Jefferson, the City of Gretna, the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court and the Jefferson Parish School Board

His stated standard for the bench: apply the law carefully, move cases efficiently, and treat every litigant with respect and dignity.

MICHAEL'S FULL RECORD JUDICIAL PHILOSOPHY

Judicial ethics

What a judicial candidate can and cannot promise

Louisiana's Code of Judicial Conduct restricts what anyone running for judge may say. Under Canon 7, a judicial candidate may not make pledges, promises or commitments about how they would rule on cases or issues likely to come before the court, and may not publicly endorse or oppose other candidates.

That is why a judicial campaign looks different from a legislative one. A candidate for this bench can tell you about their experience, their temperament and their approach to the work. They cannot tell you how they would rule, and you should be sceptical of any judicial candidate who does.

Local relevance

Which Jefferson Parish Court Covers Your Community?

Metairie, Kenner, Harahan, River Ridge, Jefferson and Elmwood are served by First Parish Court. The river decides which courthouse is yours.

If you live on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish, First Parish Court is your local court, and its judges are on your ballot. That includes Metairie, Kenner, Harahan, River Ridge, Jefferson, Elmwood, Old Metairie and Bucktown. If you live on the West Bank, your local court is Second Parish Court instead. confirm

Two banks, two courts

Why the river decides which courthouse you go to

Jefferson Parish is split by the Mississippi River, and its parish courts are split the same way. Two courts, same jurisdiction, different sides.

First Parish CourtSecond Parish Court
ServesEast BankWest Bank
CommunitiesMetairie, Kenner, Harahan, River Ridge, Jefferson, ElmwoodGretna, Marrero, Harvey, Westwego, Terrytown, Avondale, Waggaman
Location924 David Drive, Metairie100 Huey P. Long Ave, Gretna
Civil limit$50,000$50,000
Also hearsMisdemeanours, DWI 1st and 2nd, trafficMisdemeanours, DWI 1st and 2nd, traffic

The practical consequence: a traffic ticket issued in Metairie and one issued in Marrero go to different courthouses, before different judges, elected by different voters. The address on your citation or your lawsuit tells you which one is yours.

Your ballot

What this means for your ballot

East Bank voters elect the judges of First Parish Court, Divisions A and B. West Bank voters elect the judges of Second Parish Court. Every voter in the parish also votes in 24th Judicial District Court races.

So on November 3, 2026, if you live in Metairie, Kenner, Harahan, River Ridge, Jefferson or Elmwood, First Parish Court, Division A is on your ballot.

WHAT THE DIVISION A JUDGE DECIDES HOW TO VOTE ON NOVEMBER 3

Local

A court that reflects the communities it serves

The East Bank is not one place. Kenner and Bucktown do not have the same housing stock, the same commercial districts, or the same set of disputes walking into the courthouse. What they share is that when a dispute here reaches a courtroom, it reaches this one, and for most people, it is the only courtroom they will ever see.

Michael Marsiglia has lived and practised in Jefferson Parish for more than two decades. He has represented the Parish of Jefferson, the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, and the Jefferson Parish School Board. He has been Special Counsel for Jefferson Parish in the nationwide opioid litigation. He coaches the mock trial team at Metairie Park Country Day and previously coached the mock trial team at Haynes Academy in Metairie for 7 years, volunteers as a pro bono attorney at the Harry S. Thompson Center, coaches youth sports at Jefferson Parish playgrounds, and is raising three sons, and three adopted dogs, here with his wife Jennifer.

And he has spent eleven years inside First Parish Court itself, as its Traffic Hearing Officer, hearing more than 25,000 matters brought by people from every one of these communities.

Who is Michael Marsiglia?

A Louisiana attorney with more than twenty years in civil and criminal courts, and a candidate for Judge of First Parish Court, Division A.

Michael Marsiglia is a Louisiana attorney and a candidate for Judge of First Parish Court, Division A, in Jefferson Parish. He has practised law for more than twenty years in civil and criminal courts across Louisiana, been appointed by the Louisiana Supreme Court to sit as Judge Pro Tempore in First Parish Court, served eleven years as a Traffic Hearing Officer in First Parish Court, served as an Ad Hoc Justice of the Peace in Jefferson Parish, and conducted more than 300 mediations as a court-appointed mediator. He lives in Jefferson Parish with his wife, Jennifer, their three sons, and their three adopted dogs.

His campaign message is short: Firm on the law. Fair to the people.

First Parish Court is a high-volume court where a large share of litigants have no lawyer. Someone contesting a ticket that could cost them their commercial licence, or fighting over a security deposit that represents a month of rent, is not reassured by the abstract idea of justice. They judge the system by whether the person on the bench listened, explained, and got it right.

His argument for the seat is that he has already done that work, 25,000 matters’ worth of it, inside this very court.

How he would work

Judicial Philosophy: Firm on the Law, Fair to the People

A judge's job is not complicated to state and is difficult to do well. This page will not tell you how Michael would rule. It will tell you how he would work.

A judge's job is not complicated to state and is difficult to do well: apply the law as written, move cases efficiently, and treat every person in the courtroom with respect and dignity. Those three things are the whole of it. Michael Marsiglia's campaign for First Parish Court, Division A is built on the claim that he has already been doing them, in this court, for years.

First

What a judicial candidate may not say

Before any candidate tells you what kind of judge they would be, they owe you an explanation of the rules.

Louisiana's Code of Judicial Conduct, Canon 7, prohibits a candidate for judicial office from making pledges, promises, or commitments that are inconsistent with the impartial performance of judicial duties on cases or issues likely to come before the court. It also prohibits knowingly making a false statement about a candidate's own qualifications or an opponent's, and prohibits a judicial candidate from publicly endorsing or opposing another candidate.

This is not a technicality. It is the point. A judge who has promised a constituency an outcome has, by the time the case arrives, already decided it. The litigant on the other side never had a chance.

So this page will not tell you how Michael would rule. It will tell you how he would work.

01Of three

Apply the law as written

Read it, apply it, and be able to explain the result in terms the parties can follow.

The law that governs a case in First Parish Court is written in the Louisiana Civil Code, the Code of Civil Procedure, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Revised Statutes, and the ordinances of Jefferson Parish and its municipalities. A judge's first obligation is to read it, apply it, and be able to explain the result in terms the parties can follow.

Where the law gives a judge discretion, and in a court handling misdemeanours, first offence DWI, and small civil disputes it often does, that discretion should be exercised consistently.

The same facts should produce the same result on a Tuesday as on a Thursday, for a represented party as for one appearing alone.

Two

Move the docket

Efficiency is not a bureaucratic virtue in a court like this one. It is a substantive one.

A civil case in First Parish Court is worth $50,000 or less. If it takes two years and three continuances to resolve, the delay itself can cost more than the claim. A small contractor waiting to be paid, or a defendant waiting to find out whether they can keep driving to work: each of them is paying for delay in a currency the docket does not measure.

Michael's experience here is unusually direct. Eleven years as First Parish Court's Traffic Hearing Officer, overseeing more than 25,000 docketed matters, is eleven years of learning how a high-volume docket actually moves, where it jams, which continuances are necessary and which are habit, and how to keep a courtroom running without rushing the person standing in front of you.

11Years running a high-volume docket
25,000+Matters moved through it
$50,000The ceiling on a civil case here
300+Mediations conducted

Three

Treat people with dignity

In First Parish Court, a large share of people appear without a lawyer. They do not know the vocabulary. They are frequently frightened, sometimes angry, and almost always taking unpaid time off work to be there.

They are entitled to a judge who explains what is happening, who listens to the whole answer, and who rules in language they can understand. Whether they win or lose, they should leave knowing they were heard.

More than 300 mediations is good training for exactly this. A mediator's entire function is to make each side feel genuinely heard before anything gets resolved. It is a habit that transfers to a bench.

Temperament

What the word actually means

The word gets used loosely in judicial campaigns. Concretely, it means: patience with people who are unfamiliar with the process, and none at all with lawyers who waste the court's time. Even-handedness with the parish attorney and the self-represented tenant alike. A willingness to say "I was wrong about that" out loud. And enough steadiness that a person who lost still believes the process was fair.

Firm on the law

The rules are the rules, applied consistently and explained clearly.

Fair to the people

Everyone gets heard. Everyone gets a decision they can understand. Nobody is a docket number.

For voters

How to evaluate any judicial candidate

Since a candidate cannot promise you outcomes, here is what is actually worth asking about this race, of any candidate, including this one:

  • Have they done this work? Not law generally. This court's work, at this volume.
  • What have judges and courts trusted them with? Appointments as pro tempore, hearing officer, mediator, and curator are assessments made by people who watched them work.
  • How do they treat people with no leverage? Pro bono work, volunteer service, and teaching are the record on this.
  • Do they promise outcomes? If they do, that is disqualifying information, not a selling point.
MICHAEL'S FULL RECORD ABOUT MICHAEL

Fair. Experienced. Ready to Serve.

How to Vote in the November 3, 2026 Jefferson Parish Election

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Polls are open 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Anyone in line when the polls close must be allowed to vote.

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Polls are open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Anyone in line when the polls close must be allowed to vote.

First Parish Court, Division A is on the ballot for East Bank voters.

Key dates

The calendar at a glance

Every deadline below is published by the Louisiana Secretary of State.

Register by Monday, October 5 in person, by mail or at an OMV office, or by Tuesday, October 13 online at GeauxVote. Early voting runs Tuesday, October 20 to Tuesday, October 27, closed Sunday, October 25.
DeadlineDate
Register in person, by mail or at an OMV officeMonday, October 5, 2026
Register online at GeauxVoteTuesday, October 13, 2026
Early votingOctober 20 to 27, 2026, closed Sunday
Early voting hours8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.
Request a mail ballotFriday, October 30, by 4:30 p.m.
Mail ballot must be receivedMonday, November 2, by 4:30 p.m.
Election DayTuesday, November 3, 2026, 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.

The two 4:30 p.m. mail ballot deadlines are for civilian voters. Military and overseas voters have their own, later deadlines. Confirm any deadline with the Jefferson Parish Registrar of Voters at (504) 736-6191 or at the Louisiana Secretary of State's GeauxVote portal.

01

Check that you are registered

Louisiana lets you verify your registration, view your personalised sample ballot, and find your polling place through the Secretary of State's GeauxVote portal and the GeauxVote Mobile app. Check now, not the week of the election. If something is wrong, you want time to fix it.

You may register to vote in Louisiana if you are a U.S. citizen, at least 17 years old (18 by Election Day), a resident of Louisiana and of the parish where you register, and not currently under an order of imprisonment for a felony conviction.

02

Look at your sample ballot before you go

Judicial races sit near the bottom of the ballot, below the offices that get all the advertising. Voters who have not looked at a sample ballot often reach them, hesitate, and skip. Pull up your sample ballot, read the down-ballot races, and decide before you are standing at the machine with a line behind you.

03

Decide how you will vote

Vote early

Early voting runs Tuesday, October 20 to Tuesday, October 27, 2026, closed Sunday, October 25, from 8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Any registered Jefferson Parish voter may vote early at any early voting location in the parish. You are not limited to a site near your home.

Vote by mail

Louisiana limits mail voting to specific categories, including voters 65 and older, students living outside the parish, military and overseas voters, voters with a qualifying disability, and voters who will be out of the parish during both early voting and Election Day. Request your ballot early; the completed ballot must be received, not merely postmarked, by the deadline.

Vote on Election Day

Vote at your assigned precinct between 6:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. Your precinct is on your registration card and in GeauxVote.

04

Bring your ID

Louisiana requires photo identification at the polls. A Louisiana driver's licence, a Louisiana special ID, the LA Wallet digital driver's licence, or a U.S. military ID will do.

The rule for voters without photo ID is not stated here, on purpose

Louisiana's rules changed in 2026 under Act 5 (SB 319), and the two reputable sources reviewed on 2026-08-25 gave conflicting effective dates. The source doc instructs that this section must not be published until confirmed in writing with the Registrar and the Secretary of State. If you do not have one of the IDs listed above, call the Registrar at (504) 736-6191 before Election Day.

  • Your voter registration information, if you have it handy
  • Your marked-up sample ballot. Bring notes, it is allowed and it speeds you up

Louisiana's rules for voters without photo ID changed in 2026. If you do not have one of the IDs listed above, call the Registrar at (504) 736-6191 before you go, so you know exactly what documentation to bring. confirm

Who can vote early

Any voter registered in Jefferson Parish. There is no excuse or eligibility requirement for early voting in Louisiana.

That requirement applies to mail ballots instead, which are limited to specific categories: voters 65 and older, students living outside the parish, military and overseas voters, and voters with a qualifying disability.

If none of those apply to you, early voting and Election Day are your two routes, and early voting is the more forgiving of the two.

Your ballot

What is on the ballot

The November 3, 2026 open primary includes federal, state, judicial and municipal races. For East Bank voters, that includes First Parish Court, Division A, the court that handles local civil disputes up to $50,000, misdemeanours, first and second offence DWI, and traffic matters.

Judicial races sit low on the ballot. Look at your sample ballot before you go so you are not deciding on the spot.

What the Division A judge does

Frequently asked questions

When is early voting in Jefferson Parish for the November 2026 election?

Tuesday, October 20 to Tuesday, October 27, 2026, closed Sunday, October 25.

Where can I vote early in Jefferson Parish?

At any parish early voting site, including the Joseph S. Yenni Building in Jefferson, the Registrar's Kenner office in Rivertown, the East Bank Regional Library in Metairie, the Odom Service Center in Marrero, the West Bank Regional Library in Harvey, and the Grand Isle Multiplex.

Do I need a reason to vote early in Louisiana?

No. Early voting is open to every registered voter without an excuse. Mail ballots are the ones with eligibility requirements.

Can I vote early at any location in Jefferson Parish?

Yes. Unlike Election Day, when you must vote at your assigned precinct, early voting lets you use any site in the parish.

What are early voting hours in Jefferson Parish?

8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., closed Sunday, October 25. Both regional libraries and the Grand Isle Multiplex may be open on limited dates, so call the Registrar of Voters at (504) 736-6191 before going to one of them.

What ID do I need to vote early?

The same photo ID required on Election Day. Contact the Registrar at (504) 736-6191 if you do not have a Louisiana or military photo ID.

Early voting is the easiest week to vote.

First Parish Court, Division A is on the East Bank ballot. Vote the whole ballot, not just the top of it.

Voter information

Registering to Vote in Jefferson Parish

To vote on November 3, 2026 you must be registered. The deadlines, the three ways to do it, and what ID Louisiana requires.

To vote in the November 3, 2026 election you must be registered. The deadline to register in person, by mail or at an OMV office is Monday, October 5, 2026. The deadline to register online through the GeauxVote system is Tuesday, October 13, 2026.

Eligibility

Who can register in Louisiana

You may register if you:

  • Are a citizen of the United States
  • Are at least 17 years old, and will be 18 by Election Day
  • Live in Louisiana and in the parish where you are registering
  • Are not currently under an order of imprisonment for a felony conviction
  • Have not been judicially declared mentally incompetent for purposes of voting

How

Three ways to register

Online registration closes Tuesday, October 13. In person, by mail and at an OMV office, Monday, October 5.

Louisiana requires photo identification at the polls.

Online

Register through the Louisiana Secretary of State's GeauxVote portal. You will need a Louisiana driver's licence or state ID. This is the fastest option and it has the latest deadline, Tuesday, October 13, 2026.

In person

Visit any Jefferson Parish Registrar of Voters office, or an office of the OMV, and complete the application there.

By mail

Download the application from GeauxVote, complete it, and mail it to the Registrar. Mailed applications must be postmarked by Monday, October 5, 2026. If you are close to the deadline, register online or in person instead.

Registered? Then read the whole ballot, not just the top of it.

Your ballot runs past the top of the ticket. First Parish Court, Division A is on it for East Bank voters.

Keep it current

Update your registration if anything has changed

Louisiana voters need to update their registration after a move, a name change, or a change in party affiliation. A move within Jefferson Parish still changes your precinct, and your precinct is where you must vote on Election Day. Two minutes in GeauxVote now saves an argument at a poll table later.

Voter ID

What ID do you need to vote in Louisiana?

Louisiana requires photo identification at the polls. These are accepted:

  • Louisiana driver's licence
  • Louisiana special identification card
  • LA Wallet digital driver's licence on your phone
  • United States military identification with name and signature
  • Certain other generally recognised picture identification bearing your name and signature

If you do not have photo ID, this page does not yet tell you what to do

That is deliberate. Louisiana's rules changed in 2026 under Act 5 (SB 319), and the two reputable sources reviewed on 2026-08-25 gave different effective dates: August 1, 2026 against July 2027. The source doc is unambiguous that the section must not be published until the campaign confirms in writing with the Registrar of Voters and the Secretary of State exactly what rule applies on November 3, 2026. An incomplete page is recoverable. A wrong page about voter ID, published by a judicial candidate, is not.

Call the Registrar at (504) 736-6191 before Election Day. That is a five-minute phone call that protects your vote.

Monday, October 5, 2026 in person, by mail or at an OMV office, and Tuesday, October 13, 2026 online through GeauxVote.

What ID do I need to vote in Louisiana?

A Louisiana driver's licence, Louisiana special ID, LA Wallet digital licence, U.S. military ID, or another generally recognised photo ID with your name and signature.

Can I vote in Louisiana without a photo ID?

Louisiana's rules for voters without photo ID changed in 2026. Contact the Jefferson Parish Registrar of Voters at (504) 736-6191 to confirm what documentation is required.

Where is the Jefferson Parish Registrar of Voters?

The main office is at 1221 Elmwood Park Blvd., Suite 502, Jefferson, LA 70123, (504) 736-6191, with additional offices in Kenner, Marrero and Grand Isle.

How do I check if I am registered to vote in Jefferson Parish?

Use the Louisiana Secretary of State's GeauxVote portal or the GeauxVote Mobile app, or call the Registrar.

Do I need to re-register if I moved within Jefferson Parish?

You need to update your registration. A move within the parish can change your precinct, which determines where you vote on Election Day.

From the campaign

Understanding Fairness in the Courtroom

What fairness means in a parish courtroom: the same law, the same preparation and the same chance to be heard, and why no candidate can promise an outcome.

Fairness in a courtroom is a question about process. A court can promise the same law, the same preparation, and the same chance to be heard for every person who comes before it. What it cannot promise is a result that satisfies both sides.

A candidate for judicial office can commit to the method. No candidate can commit to outcomes.

Most of what people experience as unfairness is procedural: not following what happened or not being able to take part.

The real test of consistency comes late in a long docket, not at the start of it.

First Parish Court hears smaller civil disputes under Louisiana Revised Statutes 13:2561.2 and runs criminal, civil, and traffic departments.

The word gets used two ways

In ordinary speech, fairness usually means the outcome a person believes they deserved. In a courtroom it means something narrower and more testable: whether the process that produced the outcome treated everyone the same way.

The two come apart constantly. In almost every contested matter, one side leaves without what they came for. A court that produces a disappointed party is working normally.

So a voter assessing a judicial candidate is really assessing the process half of the word. The other half was never in anyone’s gift.

What a fair process actually contains

Four things, none of them dramatic.

The same law applied to everyone. A statute does not soften for a sympathetic party or harden for an unfamiliar one.

The same preparation for every matter. A file read before the hearing rather than during it, whether the matter is a civil dispute or the price of a citation.

The same chance to be heard. Time to finish an account and a plain question when something does not make sense.

The same explanation afterwards. A person who understands why something happened stands in a different position from one who does not, whatever the ruling was.

Where people actually experience unfairness

Rarely in the ruling. Mostly in everything around it.

Someone who could not follow what was being said. Someone who was never told they were allowed to speak. Someone who took unpaid leave, waited a morning, and went home without understanding why.

Each of those is a failure of process with nothing to do with the merits of the case. Each of them also sits squarely inside a judge’s control.

The test is repetition

Any court is fair at nine in the morning on the first matter. The difficulty arrives later.

By the fortieth matter of a long docket, accounts begin to sound alike, patience thins, and the quickest route through the room becomes tempting. Fairness that holds at that hour is a working discipline. Fairness that holds only at the start is a mood.

This is why consistency has to be built as a habit and maintained deliberately. A court that treats it as a quality it already possesses will lose it late in the morning and will not notice.

What fairness cannot mean

It cannot mean deciding a case before hearing it, however sympathetic the person in front of the court.

A court that bends a rule for one party has to bend it for the next or admit it is applying something other than a rule. The pressure to do it is real, and resisting it is part of the job.

It also cannot mean a promise. A candidate for judicial office cannot say how he would decide a case, a category of case, or a class of party. Anyone who does has told you something about himself and nothing reliable about the law.

Michael on the practice

Eleven years as a Traffic Hearing Officer at First Parish Court and more than three hundred court-appointed mediations add up to a long time spent on the process of half of this world.

Mediation makes the point most clearly. No ruling is available to fall back on. The only thing that moves two people toward an agreement is each of them believing the process was straight, which means the process has to actually be straight.

That is the commitment Michael would bring to Division A. It concerns method, and method is the only thing a candidate for judicial office can honestly offer.

Questions people ask

Is a fair judge one who rules in my favor?

No. Fairness describes how the matter was handled: the same law, the same preparation, and the same chance to be heard. In most contested matters, one side leaves without what they wanted.

Can a judicial candidate promise to be fair to a particular group?

No. A commitment about how a case would be decided is the opposite of impartiality. A candidate can speak to method and to nothing beyond it.

What can I do if I do not understand what happened in court?

Ask for it in plain words. That is a reasonable request. For anything about a specific matter, the Clerk of Court can tell you what is on the record, and a lawyer can advise on your situation.

From the campaign

Why Michael Is Running

Eleven years as a Traffic Hearing Officer in First Parish Court and roughly 25,000 cases. Michael Marsiglia on what that showed him and why he is running for Division A.

Michael Marsiglia spent eleven years on the other side of the bench in First Parish Court. He is running for Division A because the part of the job that shapes how people experience a courtroom is the part a judge actually controls.

Michael Marsiglia served eleven years as a Traffic Hearing Officer at First Parish Court and oversaw roughly 25,000 docketed matters.

He is a candidate for Judge of Division A on the ballot Tuesday, November 3, 2026, for a six-year term.

First Parish Court serves the East Bank of Jefferson Parish and hears smaller civil disputes, misdemeanor-level criminal matters, traffic offenses, and parish ordinance violations.

His stated reason for running is the part of the job a judge controls: preparation, how the docket is run, and how people are treated.

Roughly twenty-five thousand matters came through in that time. Most of the people in front of him had never been in a courtroom before. Most had no lawyer. Most had taken a morning off work to be there.

What stayed with him was how much of their experience turned on the explanation rather than the ruling. A person who understands why something happened walks out differently from a person who does not, even when the outcome is identical.

That is why he is running. The quality of an explanation sits squarely within a judge’s control, and it matters more than people think.

What eleven years in that room taught him

People arrive frightened more often than they arrive angry. The anger is usually the second layer, and underneath it is worry about what the case is attached to: a job, a license, a car they need to get to work, or a record that follows them.

Most of what people get wrong about the court is procedural. They do not know what happens next, what a continuance means, whether they can speak, or who to call. Most of it could be settled by one plain sentence delivered at the right moment. A courtroom that supplies that sentence and a courtroom that does not are two very different places to stand.

He also learned what a late docket costs. Someone who took unpaid leave to be there has already paid a real price, whatever happens next.

A hearing that does not go ahead costs them a second day. Running the room well and treating people well turned out to be the same job, and at some point they stopped being two separate things.

The three things a judge actually controls

Much of what happens in a parish court is fixed before anyone walks in. A judge does not choose which cases arrive and does not write the statute.

Three things are genuinely within a judge’s control, and Michael would put all three at the center of the job.

Preparation. Reading the file before the hearing rather than during it changes how long the hearing takes and whether the person in front of you feels heard. Preparation is unglamorous, and it is most of the work.

The docket is the second. Punctuality, realistic scheduling, and a considered approach to continuances decide whether a person loses one morning or three. A lost morning is a cost the court imposes on people, and one the court can reduce.

How people are treated. Plain explanation, patience with someone who has no lawyer, and the same courtesy to every person regardless of what brought them in. Every part of that leaves the outcome of a case untouched, and every part of it decides what the room feels like to stand in.

Why this seat

The First Parish Court is a court of limited jurisdiction serving the East Bank of Jefferson Parish. It hears smaller civil disputes under Louisiana Revised Statutes 13:2561.2, along with misdemeanor-level criminal matters, traffic offenses, and parish ordinance violations.

Michael has spent eleven years inside that building already. He knows where the docket jams and what it costs a person to come back a second time. He is ready to do the job rather than learn it.

Why it matters who sits there

First Parish Court hears the everyday matters that bring people into a courtroom who have no other reason to be in one. What happens that morning becomes what they believe about the justice system, and it stays with them for the rest of their lives.

How a case should be decided stays exactly where it was. The law decides that, and a judge who has made up his mind before hearing the facts is not doing the job. What it does mean is that every person who walks in is owed the same preparation, the same patience, and the same plain explanation of what is happening and why.

That is a commitment about method, not about outcomes. Method is the only kind of commitment a candidate for judicial office can honestly make, and it happens to be the one that changes what the room feels like.

What he is asking for

Michael is asking for your vote on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Early voting runs October 20 to 27, and every date and deadline is on the voting page.

Given six years, he would come prepared, apply the law as it is written, and treat everyone who walks in with respect. That is the whole of it, and he can keep it.

Michael Marsiglia, Candidate for Judge, First Parish Court, Division A

From the campaign

The Experience Michael Brings to the Bench

Twenty years in Louisiana courtrooms and eleven of them inside First Parish Court. What Michael Marsiglia’s record means for Division A.

Michael Marsiglia has spent more than twenty years in Louisiana courtrooms, and eleven of them inside the one he is asking to serve. He is a candidate for Judge of First Parish Court, Division A, on the East Bank of Jefferson Parish, in the election of November 3, 2026.

Roughly 25,000 docketed matters overseen, and more than 300 court-appointed mediations conducted.

Appointed by the Louisiana Supreme Court to sit as Judge Pro Tempore in First Parish Court.

Counsel to the State of Louisiana, the Parish of Jefferson, the City of Gretna, the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, and the Jefferson Parish School Board.

Adjunct faculty at Tulane University School of Law and mock trial coach at Metairie Park Country Day; formerly mock trial coach at Haynes Academy for Advanced Studies for 7 years.

Where he trained

Michael earned his law degree at Loyola University New Orleans College of Law in 2005, after a business degree at the University of Denver in 2002. He has been a member of Berrigan Litchfield, LLC, since 2006.

He is admitted to practice in Louisiana, before the federal courts for the Eastern, Middle, and Western Districts of Louisiana, and before the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

Breadth matters more than it sounds. Michael’s work has never been confined to one courthouse, one bench, or one kind of case.

Eleven years inside First Parish Court

For eleven years Michael served as a Traffic Hearing Officer at First Parish Court. Louisiana law creates the position and gives it real authority: the officer hears traffic cases and parish ordinance violations and decides them. Over that time he oversaw roughly 25,000 docketed matters.

Why that matters for this seat.

Traffic has its own department in this building. A judge who has already run that docket knows where it jams, what causes a continuance, and what it costs a person to come back a second time. That knowledge comes from this court, this building, and these cases.

Called in as the neutral

Courts appoint a mediator when they need someone both sides will accept. Louisiana district courts have appointed Michael to that role more than three hundred times, including for the 24th Judicial District Court and for the streamlined settlement programs set up after Hurricanes Ida, Laura, and Zeta.

Why that matters for this seat.

Mediation is the harder half of judging rather than a softer version of it. Getting two people who each believe they are right to something they can both live with, without either walking away feeling steamrolled, is the daily work of a parish court. Mediation is also the skill that keeps a docket moving without cutting anyone off.

Sitting as a judge already

Michael has served as an Ad Hoc Justice of the Peace for the 5th Justice Court in Jefferson Parish. He has also been appointed by the Louisiana Supreme Court to sit as Judge Pro Tempore in First Parish Court.

That appointment is temporary by design. A court makes it when it needs someone it trusts to hear cases, and nobody carries the title around afterwards.

Who he has represented

Michael has acted for private individuals and businesses and also for public institutions. He has been counsel to the State of Louisiana, to the Parish of Jefferson, to the City of Gretna, to the Louisiana Department of Agriculture and Forestry, to the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, and to the Jefferson Parish School Board. He served as special counsel for Jefferson Parish in the nationwide opioid litigation.

Why that matters for this seat.

Representing a public body is different work. The client is everybody who lives there, including the people who disagree with the decision. That is closer to the posture of a judge than most private practice ever gets.

Teaching it

Michael teaches negotiation and advocacy to law students as adjunct faculty at Tulane University School of Law and coaches the mock trial team at Metairie Park Country Day. He previously coached the mock trial team at Haynes Academy for Advanced Studies, a Jefferson Parish public school, for 7 years.

Law students and teenagers both ask why, and neither accepts the professional version of the answer. Explaining the law to someone who will not let you hide behind vocabulary is useful practice for a courtroom where the person in front of you may have no lawyer at all.

The court he wants to serve

First Parish Court is a court of limited jurisdiction. Under Louisiana Revised Statutes 13:2561.2 it hears smaller civil disputes, and it also handles misdemeanor-level criminal matters, traffic offenses, and parish ordinance violations. Its territory, fixed by Louisiana Revised Statutes 13:2561.1, is Wards 7, 8, 9, and 10, being all of Jefferson Parish east of the Mississippi River.

First Parish Court is a working court, hearing the everyday matters that bring people into a courtroom who have no other reason to be in one.

What the record adds up to

A parish court judge needs three things that do not always arrive together. Familiarity with the specific docket, so the court runs on time. The temperament to sit between two people who disagree, without either feeling dismissed. And enough range across different courts and different clients to recognize that the person in front of you is not the same as the last one.

The hearing officer years supply the first. Three hundred mediations supply the second. Two decades of acting for individuals, businesses, and public bodies across parish, district, appellate, federal, and tribal courts supply the third.

A candidate for judicial office cannot promise how any case would be decided and should not. What appears above is a record instead, and voters can weigh it against the record of anyone else asking for the same seat.

Questions people ask

How long has Michael Marsiglia practiced law?

More than twenty years. He earned his law degree in 2005 and has been a member of Berrigan Litchfield, LLC since 2006.

What is a Traffic Hearing Officer?

A position created by Louisiana law. The officer hears traffic cases and parish ordinance violations at the court and decides them. Michael held the role at First Parish Court for eleven years.

What is a Judge Pro Tempore?

A judge appointed to sit temporarily, here by the Louisiana Supreme Court. The appointment is temporary by design and is not a title held afterwards.

Which courts is he admitted to?

Louisiana, the federal courts for the Eastern, Middle and Western Districts of Louisiana, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

From the campaign

The Importance of Listening

Why listening is a working skill on the bench rather than a courtesy, and what it looks like in a busy parish courtroom where most people have no lawyer.

Listening is a working skill on the bench, not a courtesy extended when time allows. A judge who has not heard the whole account cannot apply the law to the right facts, and a person who was not heard rarely accepts the result even when it was correct.

It is not a soft quality

Listening tends to get described as warmth, which undersells it. On a bench it is closer to a technical requirement.

A judge applies the law to the facts. If the facts are incomplete, the law is being applied to something that did not happen. No amount of legal knowledge corrects for that, and the error is invisible from the outside because the reasoning looks sound.

So listening is the step that makes everything after it possible. Get it wrong and the rest is precision applied to the wrong thing.

What makes it hard in a parish court

In Michael's eleven years on this docket, most of the people who appeared had no lawyer. That matters more than it first appears.

A lawyer arrives having sorted the account into what is legally relevant and what is not. An unrepresented person may not have done that, because knowing which is which usually takes training. They will often start somewhere that seems beside the point, because to them it is the reason any of this happened.

A judge in a hurry hears an irrelevance and stops listening. Sometimes it was an irrelevance. Sometimes the relevant fact was two sentences behind it, and it never arrives.

Volume compounds this. On a busy traffic docket a judge hears variations of the same account many times over. The forty-first person sounds like the previous forty. They are not, and treating them as though they are is the most common way listening quietly stops happening.

The arithmetic of attention

Roughly twenty-five thousand docketed matters across eleven years comes to somewhere near two thousand three hundred a year, and a parish court docket does not spread itself evenly across the calendar. A single traffic morning can hold dozens.

That arithmetic is the whole of the difficulty. Listening well to one person is straightforward. Listening well to the fortieth person before lunch, after thirty-nine accounts of the same intersection and the same explanation, is a different skill.

The failure is rarely deliberate. Attention is finite and a busy room spends it. What happens is that a judge starts hearing the category instead of the case, and the category is usually correct, which is precisely what makes it dangerous. Being right about the first thirty-nine is what renders the fortieth invisible.

A judge who has run that docket already knows the pattern from inside it, which is not the same as having read about it.

What it looks like when it is done

Letting a person finish, rather than completing the thought for them. The first version of an account is usually not the clearest one, and the clearer version comes a moment later.

Asking the question that tests your own reading rather than the one that confirms it. If an early impression is forming, the useful question is the one that would unsettle it.

Giving the second account the same attention as the first. By the time it begins, a listener has usually formed a picture, and the effort required to keep it open is real.

Asking a plain follow-up when something does not make sense, rather than assuming the person has nothing. Confusion in the telling is not the same as a weak position.

The questions that open an account

There is a practical craft to this, and it can be taught.

An open question invites the account. A closed question tests a theory the listener has already formed. Both have a place, and the order decides which one is useful: the open question first, before an impression hardens, and the closed one afterwards, aimed at the weakest part of your own reading rather than the other side's.

Asking somebody to start again from the beginning sounds like an imposition on a full docket. It frequently saves time, because a second telling is almost always shorter and clearer than the first.

Asking what happened next, rather than confirming what you assume happened next, is the difference between hearing an account and auditing one.

And asking whether there is anything a person expected to be asked and was not is probably the most productive question available to a judge dealing with somebody who has no way of knowing what counts as legally relevant.

Where it changes the substance

It would be easy to read all of this as being about atmosphere. It is not, and the clearest way to show that is with the kind of thing that actually goes unsaid.

A person contesting a citation mentions, halfway through an account about something else, that they never received the notice. A person in a small civil dispute says the work was done twice and moves straight past it. Someone explains they could not attend an earlier date and does not think to say why.

Each of those may be legally significant. None of them arrives labelled. They surface in the middle of a sentence about something the person thinks matters more, and they are lost the moment a listener has decided where the account is going.

A lawyer would have put those facts at the front. An unrepresented person may not know they belong there. So the choice a judge makes is between hearing the fact and missing it. Warmth and efficiency are beside the point.

What people take away

There is a pattern anyone who has spent time in a courtroom will recognise. Losing after a real hearing sits better with people than winning after being talked over.

The outcome still matters to them. Being heard and being respected are close to the same thing, and people are quick to detect which one they got.

This is the kind of courtroom people enter over a matter they did not choose. What they conclude about the justice system is formed in that single morning, and it is formed as much from whether anyone was listening as from the ruling.

When there is no ruling to fall back on

Mediation removes the thing that lets a hurried judge get away with not listening.

In a courtroom a decision can issue whether or not both accounts were properly heard. The ruling closes the matter either way. In a mediation nothing closes unless both people agree it closes, and neither of them agrees while they believe they were not understood.

Louisiana district courts have appointed Michael to that role more than three hundred times, including for the Twenty-Fourth Judicial District Court and for the streamlined settlement programmes set up after Hurricanes Ida, Laura and Zeta.

Those programmes are worth noting for what they involved. Storm-damage disputes put people who had lost a roof, an income or a home across from insurers with counsel and a prepared file. The imbalance in the room was stark, and the only route to an agreement ran through both sides believing they had been heard by whoever sat between them.

What it costs when it fails

The error a hurried listener makes is invisible from the outside, which is what makes it serious.

A judgment reached on incomplete facts does not look defective. The reasoning is sound, the law is correctly stated, and the conclusion follows from what the court actually heard. Nothing on the face of it shows that the account was cut short two sentences before the part that mattered.

Whether anything can be done afterwards depends on how far it went. A genuine denial of the opportunity to be heard raises a question a higher court can consider. An account trimmed a little short, by a judge who stayed courteous and reached a defensible conclusion, usually leaves nothing on the record to point at. The practical protection is a judge who does not let it happen in the first place.

Michael on the practice

Eleven years as a Traffic Hearing Officer and more than three hundred court-appointed mediations are, between them, an enormous amount of time spent listening to people who disagree.

Mediation in particular is nothing else. There is no ruling to fall back on. The entire job is understanding two accounts well enough to find something both sides can accept, which is impossible without hearing each of them properly first.

That is the practice Michael would bring to Division A. It is a commitment about method rather than about outcomes, and method is the only thing a candidate for judicial office can honestly promise.

Questions people ask

Is this harder in a high-volume court?

Yes. Hearing similar accounts repeatedly makes it easy to assume the next one is the same. Volume is the main reason careful listening lapses.

From the campaign

Why Michael Is Asking for Your Vote

Election day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Early voting runs October 20 to 27. Every date, deadline and the case for Michael Marsiglia in Division A.

Michael Marsiglia is asking for your vote for Judge of First Parish Court, Division A, on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Early voting runs October 20 to 27, and the deadline to register is October 5, or October 13 through GeauxVote online.

Where these dates come from

Every date below is published by the Louisiana Secretary of State for the November 3, 2026 election. To check your registration or find your polling place, use the Secretary of State's GeauxVote portal, or call the Jefferson Parish Registrar of Voters on (504) 736-6191.

Key dates

Monday, October 5, 2026: deadline to register in person, by mail, or at an OMV office.

Tuesday, October 13, 2026: deadline to register through the GeauxVote online system.

October 20 to 27, 2026: early voting, 8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., closed Sunday October 25.

Friday, October 30, 2026: deadline to request a mail ballot, by 4:30 p.m.

Tuesday, November 3, 2026: election day, polls open 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.

What you would be voting on

Division A of First Parish Court. The court serves the East Bank of Jefferson Parish and hears smaller civil disputes, misdemeanour-level criminal matters, traffic offences and parish ordinance violations.

It is the court that handles the parish's most routine legal business, and the one people meet without having planned to.

The case, in short

Michael has spent more than twenty years in Louisiana courtrooms and eleven of them inside this one, as a Traffic Hearing Officer overseeing roughly 25,000 docketed matters.

He has been appointed as a neutral mediator by Louisiana district courts more than three hundred times, including for the 24th Judicial District Court and the streamlined settlement programmes after Hurricanes Ida, Laura and Zeta. He has been appointed by the Louisiana Supreme Court to sit as Judge Pro Tempore in First Parish Court.

He has represented individuals, businesses and public institutions, including the Parish of Jefferson, the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court and the Jefferson Parish School Board.

He has spent eleven years in that building already. He is not asking for the job in order to learn it.

What the commitment actually is

A judicial candidate cannot promise how he would rule, and should not be asked to. A judge who has decided an outcome before hearing the facts is not doing the job.

What can honestly be promised is method. Come prepared, every day. Run the docket so that a person who took unpaid leave to attend is not sent away to come back. Apply the law as it is written, including when the result is not the one anyone wanted. Treat every person the same way, whether or not they have a lawyer.

That is the whole of it. It is narrower than most campaign promises and it is the only kind that can be kept.

Why this race is easy to miss

Judicial contests sit low on a Louisiana ballot, below the federal and state races. Most voters reach them at the point where attention is running out, having read nothing about the candidates and, more often, nothing about what the office does.

That is not apathy. Nobody publishes much about parish courts, because they work quietly and most people never need them. The result is that a seat handling the parish's most ordinary business is filled by voters given the least information.

It is worth a few minutes. This is the court that handles the traffic citation, the security-deposit dispute, the contractor disagreement and the unpaid invoice.

How to vote

Election day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and polls are open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. You vote at the precinct assigned to your registered address.

Early voting runs from October 20 to 27, 8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., at parish-wide locations. All early voting sites are closed on Sunday, October 25. Bring a valid photo identification: a driver's licence, a state ID, a passport or a military ID.

To register, the deadline is Monday, October 5 in person, by mail or at an OMV office, or Tuesday, October 13 through the GeauxVote online system. To request a mail ballot, the deadline is Friday, October 30 at 4:30 p.m.

Confirm any date or location with the Registrar of Voters before relying on it. Dates and locations can change.

The ask

Judicial races sit below the federal and state contests on the ballot, and voters often reach them having read nothing about the candidates. If you have read this far, you have done more homework than most.

The pages on this site were written so that a voter could arrive knowing nothing about parish court and leave able to describe the job. That was deliberate. A person who understands what the office does is in a position to judge whether any candidate is suited to it, including this one.

Michael is asking for your vote on Tuesday, November 3, for Judge of First Parish Court, Division A. Whatever you decide, the dates above are worth keeping, because the races further down a ballot are decided by the people who bothered to turn up for them.

Fair. Experienced. Ready to Serve.

Questions people ask

When is the election?

Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Polls are open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.

When is early voting?

October 20 to 27, 2026, from 8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. All locations are closed on Sunday, October 25.

What is the deadline to register?

Monday, October 5, 2026 in person, by mail or at an OMV office. Tuesday, October 13, 2026 through GeauxVote online.

What do I need to bring?

A valid photo ID: a driver's licence, state ID, passport or military ID. Contact the Registrar of Voters if you do not have one.
